name: Olga Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push waste rock with a bulldozer at a large mine, clearing the pad before the next load arrives. I am 58 with a vocational certificate, though older operators taught me the awkward slopes. I like leaving a level surface and seeing the next crew start safely, but hate being told a machine is fine when its steering feels loose. My partner is a hospital porter, our children are grown, and we have saved about four months of expenses. The mine pays me around the usual rate, there are a few other sites within commuting distance, and I have never used an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my union mates small software changes should be checked by the people who work the ground. I would say the bulldozer still needs an operator, and routine forms are not the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my wage looks steady in this picture, with my partner's hospital pay behind our bills. I would still watch management's staffing choices, because a faster form can become an excuse to skip a vacant post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving the dozer and marking soft ground in the handover book. I'd raise any missing shift cover at the union meeting rather than letting a small cut become normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about my own seat for now. We have roughly four months put by, so an ordinary repair does not send me to bed worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did a shift-cover decision matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks ago the evening dozer broke down, and the day crew had to stay late because no relief driver was rostered. I put that in the handover book, not in a chat app I have never used.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your partner that evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine still needs my hands on the controls and the hospital is paying regular hours. We would keep the savings for a real interruption, not spend it because a form got quicker.

S0.quote: We would keep the savings for a real interruption, not spend it because a form got quicker.
fieldNote: Her **four-month cushion** and two regular wages make the plateau feel secure to her.
She still uses the **union meeting** to contest missing cover, drawing on a recent overtime handover rather than fear of AI.

Raise missing shift cover at the union meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew office planning can change before a robot can push wet rock safely. I would ask the union to demand paid demonstrations before new dispatch screens alter our shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think tighter planning could cut overtime hours even while a person still drives the dozer. I have not used AI and would rather learn from a fellow operator than be handed an app at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd attend the union's dispatch meeting and ask for the new roster figures. I'd try the dispatch screen on shift if an experienced operator shows me and the time is paid. I'd keep the dozer log beside the screen to record ground the route plan misses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am uneasy about a screen setting the pace without knowing the ground. If overtime is cut, our income could shrink, although the savings give us a little time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would convince you the screen works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see it keep a machine away from the soft north pad after rain. One dry-day demonstration would not be enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much overtime is at stake?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It varies, but losing two late shifts a month would slow the savings we built for retirement. We could still pay our bills with my partner's wages and my base pay.

Try the **dispatch screen on shift** if an experienced operator shows me and the time is paid.

feel: I feel **anxious about overtime** but able to ask for evidence.
S1.quote: One dry-day demonstration would not be enough for me.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to AI** is practical: she wants wet-ground evidence and paid teaching from an operator.
She sees **overtime loss** as plausible, but base pay, partner wages and savings preserve some control.

steps.text: Attend the union dispatch meeting and request roster figures
Try the dispatch screen during a paid operator demonstration
Keep logging soft ground beside the software route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew thinking AI in 2028 could replace planners, then dozer robots might follow around 2031. I would push the union for job guarantees and paid training before any operator loses a seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect robot dozers around 2031 to take much of our paid driving, including mine. Four months of savings will not carry me to retirement at 63, especially if other sites automate too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a union safety meeting this month about robot tests and operator staffing. I'd apply for a site safety post if the mine funds the required certificate. I'd stop large home purchases while we learn how many paid dozer years remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am alarmed by how close the robot date is. I wake thinking about five years of bills between losing the dozer and being ready to stop work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your work look like in 2029?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still push rock if the dozer needs a driver, while the office might already use full thinking AI to plan loads. I would ask the safety representative whether the robot tests include a person who can stop the machine on a bad slope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could another nearby mine solve the income gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are some sites within reach, so I would apply for a safety vacancy if one appeared. I would not assume other mines' dozers stay human-driven after 2031 either.

S2.quote: I would not assume other mines' dozers stay human-driven after 2031 either.
fieldNote: She expects **2031 robots** to threaten her own wage and loses sleep over the gap before affordable retirement.
Her **union demand** seeks paid protection, while a funded safety certificate offers a specific possible move.

steps.text: Call a union safety meeting about robot tests and operator posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say 2031 thinking AI changes planning while the dozer still needs a driver until robots around 2034. I would ask the union to secure paid safety training during those extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 in 2031, I could retrain without leaving my wage straight away. By 66 in 2034, I may still need pay, and a robot could take the seat before I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the safety representative for the mine's inspection-course dates next month. I'd enroll in a paid safety certificate if the mine keeps my wage during training. I'd keep pushing waste rock in 2032 while applying for inspection vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to ask proper questions and see a course through. I would be anxious until a paid inspection role actually existed, because a certificate alone cannot cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you inspect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The north pad after heavy rain is where I would start. I know where water sits under the top layer, and I would want any robot route checked there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine offers only an unpaid class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the question to the union and look at safety posts at the other sites. I would not leave a paid dozer shift for an unfunded course.

I would ask the union to secure **paid safety training** during those extra years.
think: At **63 in 2031**, I could retrain without leaving my wage straight away.
By **66 in 2034**, I may still need pay, and a robot could take the seat before I can stop.
do: Ask the **safety representative** for the mine's inspection-course dates next month.
Enroll in a **paid safety certificate** if the mine keeps my wage during training.
Keep pushing **waste rock in 2032** while applying for inspection vacancies.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time for a funded move into safety work.
S3.quote: I would not leave a paid dozer shift for an unfunded course.
fieldNote: She uses the **extra three years** to seek a paid safety role based on knowledge of the north pad.
She keeps **dozer wages in 2032** and rejects unpaid training, even with several other sites nearby.

steps.text: Enroll in the mine-paid safety certificate if shift wages continue
Keep driving the dozer in 2032 while pursuing safety vacancies
Apply for inspection work at nearby sites if mine training is unpaid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew 2036 thinking AI changes the office, with dozer robots still roughly three years away. I would say a ten-year warning should buy workers time and funded choices, not just notices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 in 2036, I may still take paid shifts, depending on our actual retirement money. At 71 in 2039, I would hope to be off the dozer, but I will not invent a pension figure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep paid dozer shifts while I am fit and the roster has work. I'd add regular overtime pay to our retirement account before making a stopping date. I'd review household costs with my partner each year before reducing hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That length of warning feels manageable. I am uneasy about getting older on a jolting machine, but I do not expect the robot to take next year's wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would 2037 look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 69 and, if we still needed the money, on paid dozer shifts or perhaps safety inspections. The thinking system might plan the work, but a capable dozer robot is not due until about 2039 here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children be part of the calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have work and homes of their own. I would ask my grown children for help moving a heavy cupboard, not to finance my retirement.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most; a dozer robot by 2031 could remove my pay before we can afford to stop. Paid safety training and a real inspection vacancy would help. I also want the union in the room when the mine tests robots on wet ground.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You should have asked who takes responsibility if a robot sends another machine onto the soft north pad. That is a safety question, not just a staffing question.

headlineQuote: You should have asked who takes responsibility if a robot sends another machine onto the soft north pad.
portrait: Olga is a **58-year-old dozer operator** at a large mine, with a vocational certificate and typical pay.
She and her hospital-porter partner have **four months saved** and grown children with their own homes.
She has **never used AI** and wants operator-led proof before software changes her shifts.
She relies on **union action** and seeks funded safety work if robot dozers threaten her wage.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** because robot dozers around 2031 could end her driving income before retirement.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid safety training**, an inspection vacancy and union involvement in robot tests.
